standard_prerequisites.name: Transport plans and their concatenation
standard_prerequisites.statement: A transport plan is a measure on a product with prescribed marginals, and the concatenation of two plans is defined by a disintegration whose expression is numbered eq:concatenation3.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the operation whose behaviour is analysed.

standard_prerequisites.name: Atoms and the intervals they merge
standard_prerequisites.statement: The atoms of the measure determine intervals of quantile levels on which the quantile function is constant, and A is their union.
standard_prerequisites.use: They are the sets on which the constancy condition is imposed.

standard_prerequisites.name: Integral inequality for increasing functions
standard_prerequisites.statement: For positive bounded increasing functions the mean of the product dominates the product of the means, with equality only when one factor is constant.
standard_prerequisites.use: It converts the sign of each summand into the constancy condition.

core_obligations: Disintegrate the concatenation using its numbered expression and rewrite the difference between the two plans as a sum of integrals over the intervals attached to the atoms of the measure (source lines 1940-1956).

Apply the integral inequality for increasing functions on each such interval, whose integrands are increasing because both plans have increasing kernel, and conclude that equality holds exactly when one of the two kernel functions is constant there (source line 1957).
Repeat the same computation for the composition with measurable maps under that constancy condition (source lines 1958-1966).

proof_roadmap.step: Disintegrate the concatenation and reduce the difference to a sum over the atoms.
Apply the integral inequality on each atom interval and characterise equality by constancy.
Repeat the computation for the second assertion.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 1922-1938, original Lemma 4.18: for a measure with quantile function g and atoms b_i with the intervals A_i they merge, the concatenation of the coupling with the two transport plans equals the plain composition exactly when on each A_i at least one of the two kernel functions is constant, and under that same hypothesis an identity holds for the compositions with measurable maps. The proof (source lines 1940-1967) is a disintegration computation that the statement hides entirely: the concatenation is rewritten through its numbered expression, the difference of the two plans is reduced to a sum of integrals over the atom intervals, and the sign of each summand is decided by the integral inequality for increasing functions, which is also what converts the equality case into the constancy condition; the second assertion repeats the computation under that condition.
